title: II. He Gets Rid Of His Eldest Son
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: You can easily picture what sort of father such a man would make, and how he would raise his children. He behaved exactly as you would expect. He abandoned the child of his marriage to Adelaïda Ivanovna entirely. It was not malice, and not resentment over his marriage; he simply forgot him. All the time he was wearing everyone out with his tears and complaints and turning his house into a sink of debauchery, a faithful family servant, Grigory, took the three-year-old Mitya under his wing. If Grigory hadn’t looked after him, nobody would even have changed the baby’s little shirt.

As it happened, the boy’s relatives on his mother’s side forgot him too, at first. His grandfather was dead. His widow, Mitya’s grandmother, had moved to Moscow and was gravely ill. The daughters were all married. So for almost a year Mitya stayed with old Grigory and lived with him in the servant’s cottage. Even if his father had remembered him (he could hardly have been altogether unaware that the boy existed), he would have sent him back to the cottage anyway, since a child would only have got in the way of his debauchery. Then a cousin of Mitya’s mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, returned from Paris. He lived abroad for many years afterwards, but at that time he was quite a young man and stood out among the Miüsovs as a man of enlightened ideas and European culture, who had lived in the capitals and abroad. Late in life he became a Liberal of the kind common in the forties and fifties. Over his career he had met many of the most Liberal men of his day, in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally. In his old age he loved to describe the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he had very nearly fought on the barricades himself. It was one of the fondest memories of his youth. He owned an independent property of about a thousand souls, reckoning in the old way. His splendid estate lay on the edge of our little town and bordered the lands of our famous monastery. Almost as soon as he inherited it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch started an endless lawsuit against the monastery over fishing rights in the river or wood-cutting in the forest, I don’t know which. He saw it as his duty, as a citizen and a man of culture, to open an attack on the “clericals.” He heard the whole story of Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom, of course, he remembered, and in whom he had once taken an interest. When he learned that Mitya existed, he stepped in, for all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He met Fyodor Pavlovitch for the first time and told him bluntly that he wanted to take over the child’s education. Long afterwards he used to tell, as a telling detail, that when he began to speak of Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch stared for some time as if he didn’t understand which child was meant, and even seemed surprised to hear he had a little son in the house. The story may be exaggerated, but it must have been something like the truth.

All his life Fyodor Pavlovitch loved to act, to take on some unexpected role suddenly, sometimes for no reason at all and even to his own obvious disadvantage, as in this case. Many people have this trait, though, and some of them are very clever, unlike Fyodor Pavlovitch. Pyotr Alexandrovitch pushed the matter through energetically. He was named joint guardian of the child with Fyodor Pavlovitch. The boy had a small property, a house and land, left to him by his mother. Mitya did indeed pass into this cousin’s keeping. But the cousin had no family of his own, and as soon as he had secured the income from his estates he was in a hurry to get back to Paris. So he left the boy with one of his cousins, a lady in Moscow. Then, settled permanently in Paris, he forgot the child too, especially once the February Revolution broke out, which left an impression on him that he remembered for the rest of his life. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya went to live with one of her married daughters. I believe he changed homes a fourth time later. I won’t go into that now, because I shall have a great deal to tell later about Fyodor Pavlovitch’s firstborn. For now I must stick to the most essential facts about him, without which I could not begin my story.

To begin with, this Mitya, or rather Dmitri Fyodorovitch, was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s three sons who grew up believing he had property and would be independent when he came of age. His boyhood and youth were unsettled. He didn’t finish at the gymnasium. He got into a military school, then went to the Caucasus, was promoted, fought a duel, was reduced to the ranks, won promotion again, lived wildly and spent a good deal of money. He received no income from Fyodor Pavlovitch until he came of age, and until then he ran up debts. He saw his father and met him for the first time when he came of age. He had come to our neighborhood on purpose to settle with him over his property. He seems not to have liked his father. He stayed only a short time and hurried away. All he had got was a sum of money and an agreement for future payments from the estate. About the estate’s income and value he could not (this is worth noting) get any statement from his father on that occasion. Fyodor Pavlovitch noticed then, for the first time (this too should be noted), that Mitya had a vague and exaggerated idea of his property. Fyodor Pavlovitch was perfectly pleased with this, as it suited his own plans. He concluded only that the young man was frivolous, unruly, violent in his passions, impatient and dissipated, and that he would be content as long as he got ready money, though only for a short time, of course. So Fyodor Pavlovitch began to exploit this, sending him small handouts now and then, in installments. In the end, four years later, Mitya lost patience and came to our little town a second time to settle accounts with his father once and for all. To his amazement, he found he had nothing. Even getting an account was difficult. He had received the whole value of his property in cash from Fyodor Pavlovitch and might even be in debt to him. By various agreements that he had entered into of his own free will at various earlier dates, he had no right to expect anything more. And so on, and so on. The young man was stunned. He suspected deceit and fraud and was almost out of his mind. And this very situation led to the catastrophe, the story of which is the subject of my first introductory tale, or rather its outward side. But before I come to that tale, I must say a little about Fyodor Pavlovitch’s other two sons and where they came from.
